chunks.text: 3D generative models. Deep generative modeling for 3D shapes has advanced across a range of representations, including point clouds, voxels, meshes, and implicit fields [ 25 ] . Early point-set methods, such as PointFlow [ 26 ] , modeled shape distributions with hierarchical continuous normalizing flows, while ShapeGF [ 2 ] learned gradient fields whose sampling procedure recovers surface geometry. Diffusion models then became a dominant paradigm for 3D shape synthesis: PVD [ 32 ] formulated denoising diffusion directly on point clouds, LION [ 29 ] moved diffusion to a hierarchical latent space to improve fidelity and enable downstream manipulations, and DiT-3D [ 18 ] showed that plain diffusion transformers can serve as competitive 3D generators. In parallel, conditional systems such as Point-E [ 20 ] and Shap-E [ 9 ] expanded generation beyond unconditional shape synthesis, while GET3D [ 4 ] demonstrated high-quality textured mesh generation from image collections. More recently, topology-aware 3D diffusion has begun to incorporate persistent homology(PH) features as global structural cues [ 6 ] . This paper introduces a new approach based on the Hilbert–Multifractal Conditioning method, which injects Hilbert-serialized multifractal descriptors as multi-scale structural priors for point-cloud generation. Whereas persistent homology captures connected components, loops, and voids, HMC captures voxel mass distribution, density heterogeneity, and local spatial neighborhoods. Furthermore, persistent homology uses a dedicated topological encoding pipeline, while Hilbert sequences can be directly processed by sequence models and bottleneck fusion modules, which can exploit prior information about the reference density structure to improve generation quality and diversity. 3.1 Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) for 3D Point Clouds Following Mo et al. [18] and Guan et al.

We use point clouds X ∈ ℝ N × 3 X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 3} , where N N represents the number of points with x , y , z x,y,z coordinates, sampled uniformly from a given surface to represent 3D shapes. HilbertGen-3D initially voxelizes it as input v i ∈ ℝ V × V × V × 3 v_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times V\times V\times 3} where V V represents the grid resolution.

Following DiT-3D [ 18 ] , the voxel grid is then divided into non-overlapping patches of size p × p × p p\times p\times p , resulting in a sequence of patch tokens s i ∈ ℝ L × d s_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times d} with length L = ( V / p ) 3 L=(V/p)^{3} and embedding dimension d d that serve as the primary input to the DiT backbone, where the embedding is realized via a learned linear projection. In Section 4.1 , we introduce locality-preserving density signals along Hilbert curves at different scales for local information and generalized dimension for global information, which we process through a lightweight transformer encoder to generate the HMC tokens. These tokens pass through a bottleneck structure with multiple transformer blocks (DiT block) that employ self-attention to update the features, which we discuss in detail in Section 4.2 . Finally, to achieve denoising in the point cloud space, the voxelized representation is converted back to the original point cloud format via devoxelization, yielding the denoised point cloud. 4.1 Hilbert serialization and generalized dimensions Multi-scale voxel measures. The Hilbert-ordered sequences ( 3 ) and HMC descriptors ( 7 ) are encoded through two separate branches. Each sequence c s c_{s} is split into consecutive windows of length w w , with zero-padding of the final window when necessary. The window embeddings include position, scale, and valid-length information. A lightweight Transformer processes the concatenated multi-scale window embeddings to produce the HMC tokens C = E seq ​ ( { c s } s ∈ 𝒮 ) ∈ ℝ M × d , C=E_{\mathrm{seq}}\!\left(\{c_{s}\}_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}, where M = ∑ s ∈ 𝒮 ⌈ R s 3 w ⌉ M=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\left\lceil\frac{R_{s}^{3}}{w}\right\rceil and E seq E_{\mathrm{seq}} denotes the learned encoder. The resulting embedding C C retains its window index, although self-attention can incorporate context from other windows and scales. During training, both raw inputs are extracted from the clean shape. Bottleneck fusion via perceiver resampler Directly injecting all HMC tokens into the denoising transformer can be inefficient. The number of Hilbert sequence tokens grow with the number of scales and with the voxel resolution, while voxelized point clouds are sparse and often produce many weakly informative patch tokens. Inspired by the bottleneck design of TopoDiT-3D [ 6 ] , we use a Perceiver-style resampler to fuse local geometry tokens with global and multi-scale HMC tokens through a fixed-size latent interface. We introduce K b K_{b} learnable bottleneck latents B ∈ ℝ K b × d B\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{b}\times d} , where K b ≪ L + M K_{b}\ll L+M . The bottleneck first compresses the concatenated local and HMC context: B ← B + XAttn ⁡ ( B , [ H t ; C ~ ] ) , B\leftarrow B+\mathrm{XAttn}\big(B,\;[H_{t};\widetilde{C}]\big), (12) where C ~ = P C ​ ( C ) \widetilde{C}=P_{C}(C) and P C P_{C} is the learned projection. The resulting latent tokens B B are updated by DiT blocks using a t a_{t} for AdaLN modulation. The processed B B is then used to update the geometry tokens: H t ← H t + XAttn ⁡ ( H t , B ) . H_{t}\leftarrow H_{t}+\mathrm{XAttn}\big(H_{t},B\big). (13) This module serves two purposes. First, it adaptively filters redundant sparse-voxel tokens and keeps the main DiT computation independent of the full HMC token length. Second, it provides a compact fusion interface between local geometric features and Hilbert-multifractal structural priors. In this way, the denoiser receives multi-scale shape information without attending directly to all local and condition tokens at every layer. 4.2 Integration into Diffusion Architectures We retain the voxel patchification and pointwise output structure of DiT-3D [ 18 ] and use the bottleneck design of TopoDiT-3D [ 6 ] to inject HMC conditions.

In this section, we evaluate HilbertGen-3D and conduct sensitivity experiments to investigate the effectiveness of the bottleneck structure and topological information within the point cloud data. 5.1 Experiment Setup Dataset. In line with most prior work [ 26 , 16 , 1 , 32 , 29 , 18 , 6 ] , we use the ShapeNet dataset as the benchmark for 3D point cloud generation [ 3 ] . ShapeNet comprises 51,127 51,127 shapes across 55 55 classes. Following prior work, we train HilbertGen-3D on the Chair, Airplane, and Car categories. We show further results on Lamp and Vessel in Appendix A . Evaluation. Following prior work [ 18 , 6 ] , we use Chamfer Distance (CD) and Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) to compute 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) and Coverage (COV). The 1-NNA metric computes the leave-one-out accuracy of a 1-Nearest Neighbor classifier, with lower scores signifying superior generative performance in both quality and diversity. Coverage (COV), on the other hand, quantifies the proportion of ground-truth reference point clouds that correspond to at least one generated shape. Although COV is highly sensitive to mode dropping and serves as an effective measure of diversity, it does not assess the geometric quality of the generated point clouds. Implementation. To ensure consistency, we adopt the implementation from DiT-3D and TopoDiT-3D [ 18 , 6 ] . The input voxel size is set to 32 × 32 × 32 × 3 ​ ( V = 32 ) 32\times 32\times 32\times 3(V=32) , and we train the models for 10,000 10,000 epochs using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} and a batch size of 512 512 . In our experiments, we set T = 1000 T=1000 and use S / 4 S/4 configuration with a patch size p = 4 p=4 . Specifically, we pick the scale set 𝒮 = { 3 , 4 , 5 } \mathcal{S}=\{3,4,5\} and momentum set 𝒬 = { 1 , 2 , 3 } \mathcal{Q}=\{1,2,3\} .

We pick the window length w = 64 w=64 to generate the HMC token and set the depth of the perceiver resampler to 4 with bottleneck latent dimension K b = 128 K_{b}=128 . After training the DiT backbone, we report metrics from two versions of the proposed algorithm: in the first version, we construct a bank of HMC tokens from the training data, which is then randomly sampled from during generation; in the second version, we separately train a variational autoencoder on the training data and then use the VAE to generate HMC tokens during inference. The VAE baseline uses latent dimension 64, encoder hidden widths ( 2048 , 1024 , 512 ) (2048,1024,512) with SiLU activations, and a decoder with the reversed hidden widths. Its objective uses β VAE = 0.05 \beta_{\mathrm{VAE}}=0.05 and unit reconstruction weights. VAE training uses AdamW with initial learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} , zero weight decay, batch size 256, cosine learning-rate decay, gradient clipping at 1, and 2000 epochs. 5.2 Comparison to Prior Works We compare HilbertGen-3D with representative point-cloud generative models in Table 1 , reporting two variants: Ours-VAE uses VAE-generated HMC conditions, while Ours-bank uses bank-sampled HMC conditions. Both variants improve 1-NNA relative to TopoDiT-3D [ 6 ] across all three categories under both CD and EMD. Here, improvements in 1-NNA refer to reductions in the absolute distance from 50, rather than decreases in the raw accuracy. Coverage gains are more dependent on the category and conditioning source, with neither variant uniformly outperforming the other. For Chair, Ours-VAE achieves the best 1-NNA among all compared methods, reaching 50.25 under CD and 48.42 under EMD. These values reduce the absolute distance from 50 by 0.88 and 1.89 percentage points, respectively, compared with TopoDiT-3D.

Following prior work [ 18 , 6 ] , we use Chamfer Distance (CD) and Earth Mover’s Distance (EMD) to compute 1-Nearest Neighbor Accuracy (1-NNA) and Coverage (COV). Coverage (COV), on the other hand, quantifies the proportion of ground-truth reference point clouds that correspond to at least one generated shape. Although COV is highly sensitive to mode dropping and serves as an effective measure of diversity, it does not assess the geometric quality of the generated point clouds. Implementation. The ablations therefore support the combined design without establishing that every component improves every evaluation criterion. 6 Conclusion In this work, we presented HilbertGen-3D, a diffusion framework for point cloud generation based on Hilbert–Multifractal Conditioning (HMC). Experiments suggest that HMC is a promising conditioning strategy for improving global coherence and structural fidelity in generated 3D shapes. More broadly, the proposed framework shows that locality-preserving spatial serializations together with multi-resolution scaling statistics can serve as an effective alternative to purely local conditioning schemes. On the other hand, it shall be noted that, while HilbertGen-3D can effectively generate point clouds in settings when prior information of the overall density distribution can be exploited, alternative approaches (such as persistent homology) may perform well otherwise. Future directions include distilling the diffusion model to reduce computational cost [ 27 ] and using Bayesian techniques to further improve generation accuracy [ 28 ] . Resampler depth has the largest observed effect among the parameter ranges considered. Depth 4 achieves the best 1-NNA-CD of 55.57 and the highest COV-CD and COV-EMD of 60.98 and 59.27 within this group. Compared with depth 3, it reduces the distance of 1-NNA-CD from 50 by 3.88 percentage points and increases COV-CD and COV-EMD by 4.21 and 1.29 percentage points. However, depth 3 achieves the closest 1-NNA-EMD to 50, at 53.09, compared with 53.66 for depth 4. The weaker results at depth 2 further show that performance does not improve monotonically with depth. These observations support depth 4 for the coverage and CD-based criteria in this experiment, while retaining an EMD-based 1-NNA advantage for depth 3. MLP ratio. An MLP ratio of 3 achieves the best 1-NNA-CD, 1-NNA-EMD, and COV-EMD within its group, at 55.46, 52.27, and 59.58, respectively. Relative to the ratio-4 baseline, the distances of the two 1-NNA metrics from 50 decrease by 0.11 and 1.39 percentage points, while COV-CD and COV-EMD increase by 0.19 and 0.31 percentage points.

Ratio 3.5 yields the highest COV-CD of 61.19, exceeding ratio 3 by only 0.02 percentage points. Thus, the largest tested MLP ratio is not favored by the reported means: ratio 3 improves every metric relative to the baseline and is close to the group maximum in the remaining coverage comparison. We have chosen MLP ratio of 4 in the hope that smaller step-size, larger batch size, and larger epochs would benefit a slightly more complicated model. Number of bottleneck latents. Increasing the bottleneck length does not yield uniform gains. The baseline with 128 latents attains the best 1-NNA-CD of 55.57, but the result with 96 latents is nearly identical at 55.58. In contrast, 96 latents achieves the best 1-NNA-EMD and COV-EMD, at 51.95 and 59.48. Compared with 128 latents, this reduces the EMD-based 1-NNA distance from 50 by 1.71 percentage points and increases COV-EMD by 0.21 percentage points, while COV-CD decreases by 0.23 percentage points. The 32- and 128-latent settings tie for the highest COV-CD at the reported precision, although the 32-latent setting has worse 1-NNA under both distances. The results therefore show a trade-off between bottleneck length and the different evaluation criteria, rather than a consistent advantage for the largest bottleneck. Scale selection. The full scale set 𝒮 = { 3 , 4 , 5 } \mathcal{S}=\{3,4,5\} achieves the best 1-NNA-CD and both coverage metrics within its group. However, the two-scale alternatives yield better 1-NNA-EMD, with { 3 , 5 } \{3,5\} attaining the closest value to 50 at 51.91. Compared with { 3 , 5 } \{3,5\} , the full scale set improves the CD-based 1-NNA distance by 0.47 percentage points and increases COV-CD and COV-EMD by 0.65 and 0.48 percentage points, but worsens the EMD-based 1-NNA distance by 1.75 percentage points. Accordingly, retaining all three scales favors coverage and CD-based distribution matching in this experiment, but does not improve every measure of distribution matching.

Since every tested configuration contains multiple scales, this comparison does not establish an advantage over single-scale conditioning. Moment-order selection. The baseline moment set 𝒬 = { 1 , 2 , 3 } \mathcal{Q}=\{1,2,3\} achieves the best 1-NNA-CD and COV-EMD within its group, at 55.57 and 59.27. Using only 𝒬 = { 1 } \mathcal{Q}=\{1\} gives the highest COV-CD of 61.31 and also yields a 1-NNA-EMD value closer to 50 than the baseline, at 53.11. The set { 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 } \{1,2,3,4\} achieves the best 1-NNA-EMD of 52.65, improving its distance from 50 by 1.01 percentage points relative to the baseline, but reducing COV-CD and COV-EMD by 1.67 and 0.98 percentage points. Adding moment orders therefore does not produce a monotonic improvement. The { 1 } \{1\} configuration retains the information-dimension descriptor; it should not be interpreted as removing the global HMC descriptor altogether. Interpretation and scope. The baseline provides a common reference, but the table does not identify it as uniformly optimal. In particular, MLP ratio 3 improves all four reported means relative to that reference. The groupwise comparisons also do not establish the performance of a configuration that combines the individually favorable settings, since interactions between parameter choices are not evaluated by these comparisons. These results concern Ours-Bank on Airplane under the 2000-epoch training recipe. They do not establish the same parameter preferences for Ours-VAE, other categories, or longer training schedules. The four seeds are evaluation seeds; the table does not quantify variation across independently trained models. Furthermore, without seedwise dispersion estimates, small differences such as 0.01 in 1-NNA-CD between 96 and 128 latents, or 0.02 in COV-CD between MLP ratios 3 and 3.5, should be interpreted as numerical rankings rather than evidence of statistically significant performance differences.
